context_blurb:
A living cell is a drop of water crowded with polymers, large molecules each built as a chain of small units. Four kinds do most of life's work: carbohydrates, lipids, proteins and nucleic acids. Around them lies the cell membrane, a thin, oily skin that decides what gets in and out.

Leaves make the sugar glucose, and a plant joins much of it into starch, a glucose chain stored as grains in tubers, roots and seeds. Loose glucose would dissolve in a cell's water, and water would follow it in by osmosis, flowing through the membrane toward where more is dissolved, until the cell swelled. Starch does not dissolve, so its packed grains draw no extra water into the cells.

Lipids, the fats and oils, do not dissolve in water either. An animal keeps a quick store, glycogen, a branched glucose chain in muscle and liver, but the bulk of its reserve as fat. Gram for gram, fat packs in more than twice the energy of glycogen, and it is stored dry, while each gram of glycogen holds three or four grams of water.

Ernest Overton gave the first clue to the membrane in the 1890s. He bathed living cells in some five hundred substances and timed how fast each got in. Those that mix with oil slipped in far faster than water-loving ones, whatever their size, for a fatty barrier lets through what mixes with fat. So the cell's outer boundary, Overton concluded, is a thin layer made largely of fat.

In 1925 Evert Gorter and François Grendel measured that layer. A mature mammal red blood cell has neither a nucleus nor inner membranes, so all its fat lies in its outer skin. They dissolved out that fat and spread it across water in a film one molecule deep, and it covered about double the cells' surface. So the membrane must be a double layer of fat molecules, stacked two deep. Its fat molecules, phospholipids, turn their oily tails inward and their water-loving heads out. Two errors in the pair's work roughly cancelled, and the double layer has stood.

Proteins, chains of about twenty kinds of amino acid, include antibodies, the keratin in hair and enzymes, which speed reactions. Many chemists thought proteins shapeless mixtures, varying from molecule to molecule. From 1943 to 1955 Frederick Sanger broke cattle insulin into short overlapping pieces, identified each, and fitted the overlaps together. Insulin proved to be two chains, of 21 and 30 amino acids, each in one exact order, and by extension every protein has its own sequence. That order sets each chain's folded shape.

In the 1860s Friedrich Miescher found the nucleic acid DNA, deoxyribonucleic acid, in white blood cells; Phoebus Levene later showed it to be a chain of units called nucleotides, in just four kinds. Into the 1940s most biologists took genes, the units of heredity, to be protein. Genes must hold a vast store of varied instructions, and twenty kinds of unit seemed to promise far more different chains than four. Experiments in 1944 and 1952 proved genes are DNA: four kinds of unit, in any order along a long chain, spell endless messages.

Small molecules cross the membrane by diffusion, spreading from crowded to less crowded with no energy spent. A human cell holds some thirty times more potassium than the fluid outside; potassium leaks out all the time, yet the gap lasts, because the cell pumps it back in by active transport, spending energy against the crowd. The proof is a poison such as cyanide that cuts off the cell's energy supply: the leak then wins, and the difference fades.

Water crosses membranes too. In 1748 Jean-Antoine Nollet sealed a jar of alcohol with pig's bladder tied across its mouth and sank it in water. The bladder let water in far more readily than it let alcohol out, so the jar overfilled and pushed the bladder out tight, sometimes until it burst. In the 1820s the French doctor Henri Dutrochet coined endosmose and exosmose, the roots of the word osmosis.

Osmosis is why salt kills a slug. The salt dissolves in its slime into a brine saltier than its body, and water flows out through its skin toward the salt until the slug dies of drying out; Gordon Port of Newcastle University says the salt simply draws the water out. A slug's skin lets water out very easily, while a person's lets far less through, so salt on a hand does no harm.
